author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Diagnose memory pressure and unexpected PS2 emulator restarts
summary: Separate a true process restart from a game crash or activity recreation by preserving logs, watching memory growth, testing texture and capture features independently, and reproducing under a fixed Android workload.
heroAlt: PCSX2 software-renderer OSD showing memory and timing counters for a controlled diagnostic run

sourceLabels.android-process: Android process lifetime and reclaim rules

blocks.text: Prove whether the Android process actually died

Returning to a launch screen can mean the emulator process was killed, the game crashed inside an intact process, or Android recreated the activity after a configuration event. Preserve the earliest logs, note whether the library and session state were rebuilt, and reproduce with a fixed title route. Watch for memory that climbs across area changes or after repeated savestate, capture, or texture operations.
Do not repeatedly trigger a suspected out-of-memory condition while unsaved progress is open. Back up saves and stop if the device becomes unstable or other apps lose work.
Prepare evidence before the next restart

items: A normal save before the reproducible route and a separate save backup.
Android and emulator logs captured from before launch through failure.
The exact renderer, resolution, texture, capture, and savestate settings.
Available memory observations at fixed route landmarks.
A clean baseline with unrelated heavy apps closed.

blocks.text: Separate workload growth from Android reclaim

items: 1. Cold-boot the title and record process identity or clear lifecycle markers in the log.
2. Follow the route while noting memory at each area transition.
3. After a restart, save logs immediately before relaunching anything.
4. Check for low-memory kill, allocation failure, native crash, or ordinary activity recreation evidence.
5. Repeat with capture and texture replacement disabled, leaving rendering otherwise unchanged.
6. Test repeated savestate creation or loading separately if the symptom follows those actions.
7. Run once with another known memory-heavy app open only if it is safe and needed to test reclaim sensitivity.
8. Report the smallest route and feature set that reproduces the process loss.

blocks.text: A monotonic memory climb tied to repeated operations suggests a leak or unbounded cache. An immediate allocation failure at one scene suggests a peak requirement. A process reclaimed only when backgrounded follows a different Android lifecycle path. Logs and process markers keep these cases from being merged into one generic crash report.
The report should identify the failure class and the minimum reproducible workload.

items: Logs cover the period before and after the restart.
Process death is distinguished from activity recreation and game reset.
Memory is sampled at the same route landmarks.
Optional high-memory features are tested one at a time.
Save data remains intact and backed up.
Logs start only after relaunch: reproduce with capture already active.
Several texture and capture settings change together: split the test.
Only free-memory dashboard numbers are used: include failure logs and route behavior.
The restart occurs after Android updates the app: begin a clean post-update case.

blocks.text: Return to a conservative memory profile

Disable only the feature proven to trigger the failure, restore the accepted renderer and resolution, close diagnostic capture, and cold-boot from the normal save. Keep the backup and minimal reproduction bundle until the issue is resolved.
Free RAM is intentionally used by Android

A low free-memory number alone is not proof of a leak. Android caches aggressively and reclaims processes according to importance. Prefer allocation errors, kill reasons, repeatable growth, and lifecycle evidence over a single dashboard reading.
